query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermomechanical treatment that creates a gradient microstructure with uniformly distributed ultrafine, coherent nanoprecipitates along grain boundaries and within the matrix will improve ductility and uniform deformability in refractory high-entropy alloys under dynamic loading, while retaining their high strength and impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory HEAs that exhibit very high strength and excellent impact-induced energy release but suffer from limited plasticity and strain localization (nonuniform deformability) under mechanical strain.
generation.intervention: Apply a specifically designed thermomechanical treatment (e.g., cyclic deformation with controlled cooling) to induce a gradient microstructure with a well-dispersed population of ultrafine, coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under conditions mimicking dynamic loading, such as high strain rate impacts and operational temperature ranges relevant to energetic structural materials.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient microstructure characterized by uniformly distributed ultrafine, coherent nanoprecipitates both along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The engineered gradient microstructure is hypothesized to impede localized dislocation motion and arrest strain concentration by providing uniform barriers, leading to progressive strain hardening and enhanced deformation uniformity without compromising the inherent strength or the impact-induced energy release capabilities.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated HEA is expected to show a noticeable increase in uniform ductility and more homogeneous deformation under dynamic loading, while maintaining high tensile strength and impact energy release similar to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA with a conventionally processed, uniform microstructure that exhibits limited ductility and strain localization despite high strength and energy release.
generation.boundary: The positive effect is anticipated only if the treatment precisely controls the precipitate size, distribution, and gradient structure; deviations may either nullify the ductility enhancement or adversely affect the strength and energy release, especially under extreme temperature or strain rate conditions beyond the tested range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the ductility improvement and the quantitative balance between enhanced deformability and retention of strength remains uncertain until systematic experimental validation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set will undergo the tailored thermomechanical treatment to induce the gradient microstructure, and the other set will remain as conventionally processed controls. Subject both sets to dynamic loading tests (e.g., high strain rate tensile or impact tests) under comparable environmental conditions.
measurements: Quantitative tensile ductility (uniform elongation) and strain distribution via digital image correlation or equivalent techniques
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to confirm the gradient distribution and coherence of nanoprecipitates
Tensile strength measurements to ensure no significant loss compared to control
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility and uniform deformability under dynamic loading—without a reduction in strength or impact-induced energy release—compared to the untreated control group, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The need for high-performance structural materials that can be effective under extreme conditions is one of the outstanding technological challenges in materials science. To meet this challenge, materials need to be developed that not only have higher strength and toughness but also can retain these characteristics at elevated temperatures or strain rates. The emerging concept of multiple principal element alloys, often termed high- or medium-entropy alloys (HEA/MEAs), provides these opportunities (). In particular, CrCoNi-based HEA/MEAs and their variants exhibit remarkable fracture toughness and damage tolerance over ambient-to-cryogenic temperatures due to continuous strain hardening induced by a sequence of plastic deformation mechanisms, particularly a strong effect of twinning and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) (). Because twinning is also promoted by elevated strain rates (>103/s), the mechanical properties of these alloys are expected to excel under extreme impact or shock conditions. A emerging paradigm for the development of metallic materials has been the notion of multiple-principal-element alloys, often termed as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or compositionally complex alloys (CCAs), which has presented promising pathways for seeking improved alloys within a previously unexplored compositional/phase space. Numerous mechanistic phenomena have been studied to induce significant strengthening and toughening in these alloy systems, which serve to improve their strength-ductility synergy; these include high lattice friction, interstitial solid solution, grain refinement and gradients in grain size, in situ phase transformation, and nano-precipitation. Of note here is the approach of incorporating nano-precipitates that have a positive influence on both strength and ductility. This not only results in a significant strengthening by precipitation hardening but also generates progressive multistage strain hardening that can effectively enhance ductility by delaying the onset of localized plastic instability,. AbstractCoCrNi alloys exhibit excellent strength and ductility. In this work, the CoCrNiV multi-principal alloy with single-phase fine grained (FG) structure was prepared by rolling and heat treatment. The characteristics of deformation microstructures and mechanical properties were systematically investigated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM). The results indicate that the CoCrNiV alloy successfully attains a yield strength of 1060 MPa while maintaining a uniform elongation of 24.1%. The enhanced strength originates from FG structure and severe lattice distortion induced by V addition. Meanwhile, the exceptional ductility arises from the stable strain-hardening ability facilitated by dislocations and stacking faults. The deformation mechanisms and the optimization strategies for attaining both strength and ductility are thoroughly discussed.Keywords: CoCrNiV alloy, multi-principal element alloy (MPEA), stacking fault, solid solution strengthening, fine grain (FG)

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity. decision.trend: Early studies in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) began by elucidating nanoscale and defect‐mediated deformation mechanisms (e.g., shockley partials, twinning, stacking faults) that could reconcile strength and ductility. Later, in refractory HEAs for extreme applications, researchers have focused on microstructure design through controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (PMC10213035) and dual-phase architectures (PMC11767206) to boost strength while partially alleviating ductility issues. These studies established that engineered nanoscale features (e.g., coherent precipitates, refined dual phases) are critical to deferring strain localization and preventing premature crack formation. However, although advances in composition, processing routes and precipitate control have enhanced strength and energy release, ductility and uniform deformability remain challenging without sacrificing the energy output essential for energetic structural materials.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge is to significantly improve plasticity and achieve uniform deformability (especially under high strain rates) in refractory HEAs without compromising their high strength and impact-induced energy release. Prior interventions have either led to a trade-off or could not fully address strain localization during dynamic loading.
decision.lever: Implement a tailored thermomechanical treatment that engineers a gradient microstructure with uniformly distributed ultrafine, coherent nanoprecipitates along grain boundaries and within the matrix
decision.why: By building on the trend that coherent interfaces and nanoscale precipitate control can enhance ductility without undermining strength, this approach directly targets strain localization. The hypothesis is that a gradient microstructure—with strategically positioned, fine precipitates to uniformly arrest dislocation motion and mitigate stress concentrations—will improve ductility under dynamic impact conditions while preserving the high strength and energy release capabilities observed in refractory HEAs.
